CausalChain: Circadian nutrient signals -> Timed hepatic PPARβ/δ activation (using CRISPR-based chronotherapy) -> Upregulation of lipogenic enzymes -> Enhanced and exosome-packaged synthesis of PC (18:0/18:1) -> Exosomal release into circulation -> Targeted delivery and activation of muscle PPARα -> Increased fatty acid uptake and mitochondrial β-oxidation -> Improved systemic lipid metabolism
Hypothesis: Our revised hypothesis posits that time-synchronized activation of hepatic PPARβ/δ, orchestrated through state-of-the-art gene-editing and chronotherapy interventions, drives the circadian production and exosomal packaging of bioactive PC (18:0/18:1). The targeted, exosome-mediated transport of this specific lipid to skeletal muscle leads to the activation of muscle PPARα, thereby boosting fatty acid oxidation at the mitochondrial level. This integrative mechanism, substantiated by advanced omics and real-time imaging platforms, represents a novel inter-organ regulatory axis that could be therapeutically exploited to ameliorate dyslipidemia and metabolic syndrome.
Abstract: We propose that precise, time-synchronized activation of hepatic PPARβ/δ—achieved via modern gene-editing and chronotherapy techniques—induces a circadian upregulation of lipogenic enzymes, specifically enhancing the synthesis and exosomal packaging of bioactive phosphatidylcholine (PC 18:0/18:1). This exosome-mediated delivery system ensures targeted transfer of PC (18:0/18:1) to skeletal muscle, where it binds and activates PPARα to promote fatty acid uptake and mitochondrial β-oxidation. Leveraging advanced metabolomics and single-cell transcriptomics, this inter-organ signaling mechanism offers a novel and precise therapeutic approach to correct dyslipidemia and mitigate metabolic syndrome, integrating circadian biology, nuclear receptor modulation, and lipid mediator signaling.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis suggested that circadian activation of hepatic PPARβ/δ enhances the production of PC (18:0/18:1), which then activates muscle PPARα to improve lipid metabolism. The new hypothesis retains this conceptual framework but incorporates advanced methodological approaches for precise temporal control using CRISPR-induced activation and chronotherapy. It explicitly addresses the mechanism of PC (18:0/18:1) delivery by proposing exosomal packaging as the transporter, thereby clarifying the inter-organ communication pathway. Additionally, the revised hypothesis leverages modern technologies such as metabolomics and single-cell transcriptomics, ensuring practical implementability and robust validation of each causal link in the chain.
